clinicalPearls: A heterogeneous group of subepithelial autoimmune blistering diseases with a predilection for mucous membranes and a marked tendency to scar.
The oral mucosa is most frequently involved (desquamative gingivitis is a common presenting sign), followed by ocular, nasopharyngeal, oesophageal, laryngeal and anogenital sites.
Ocular disease progresses through chronic conjunctivitis, subconjunctival fibrosis, symblepharon, forniceal shortening, entropion, trichiasis and ultimately corneal opacification and blindness.

Autoantibodies target multiple basement-membrane antigens, most commonly BP180 (particularly its C-terminus) and laminin-332; anti-laminin-332 disease carries an association with underlying malignancy.
Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional mucosa showing linear IgG, IgA and/or C3 along the basement-membrane zone is the diagnostic cornerstone; sensitivity rises with multiple biopsies.
The Nikolsky sign may be positive; healing with scarring distinguishes it clinically from bullous pemphigoid, which typically heals without scars.
Management is stratified by site and severity; high-risk (ocular, laryngeal, oesophageal, severe oral) disease warrants aggressive systemic immunosuppression to prevent irreversible scarring.
A multidisciplinary approach involving dermatology, ophthalmology, ENT, oral medicine and gastroenterology is essential for organ-threatening disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Mucous membrane pemphigoid results from autoantibodies, predominantly IgG and IgA, directed against structural components of the epithelial basement-membrane zone, chiefly the BP180 (type XVII collagen) antigen and laminin-332 (epiligrin), and less often BP230, type VII collagen and the integrin beta-4 subunit. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits inflammatory cells, causing dermo-epidermal separation within the lamina lucida. Unlike bullous pemphigoid, the inflammatory infiltrate and cytokine milieu at mucosal sites drive a fibrotic reparative response, so repeated cycles of blistering and healing produce progressive submucosal scarring. The predilection for particular target antigens correlates loosely with clinical phenotype, and anti-laminin-332 reactivity is linked to paraneoplastic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (chronic ocular sequelae)
additionalInvestigations: perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (linear IgG/IgA/C3 at the basement-membrane zone)
lesional biopsy for histopathology (subepithelial split with mixed infiltrate)
indirect immunofluorescence on salt-split skin (epidermal vs dermal binding)
serum ELISA/immunoblot for BP180, BP230 and laminin-332 antibodies
slit-lamp ophthalmological assessment and conjunctival forniceal measurement
nasendoscopy and laryngoscopy for upper-airway involvement
age-appropriate malignancy screening when anti-laminin-332 antibodies are detected
redFlags: ocular involvement with progressive symblepharon or forniceal shortening threatening sight
laryngeal or supraglottic disease causing stridor or airway compromise
oesophageal stricture with dysphagia and risk of aspiration or malnutrition
anti-laminin-332 antibodies signalling possible occult malignancy
rapidly progressive scarring despite first-line therapy
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and relapsing; with early aggressive immunosuppression, scarring can often be arrested, but established fibrosis is irreversible and untreated organ-threatening disease may lead to blindness, airway stenosis or oesophageal stricture.
pitfalls: Attributing desquamative gingivitis to poor oral hygiene or dental disease and delaying immunofluorescence biopsy.
Taking the biopsy from an ulcerated (rather than perilesional) site, yielding a false-negative direct immunofluorescence.
Overlooking asymptomatic early ocular disease because cutaneous involvement is minimal or absent.
Failing to screen for malignancy when laminin-332 antibodies are identified.
Under-treating so-called low-risk oral disease that later extends to high-risk sites.

management: Risk-stratified immunosuppression: topical or intralesional corticosteroids for limited oral disease, escalating to systemic corticosteroids with a steroid-sparing agent such as dapsone, mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine
Cyclophosphamide with corticosteroids, or rituximab and intravenous immunoglobulin, for organ-threatening ocular, laryngeal or oesophageal involvement
Screen for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency before dapsone and monitor blood counts during treatment
Meticulous oral hygiene and topical care to control desquamative gingivitis, with ocular surface lubrication and management of trichiasis and symblepharon
Investigate for occult malignancy where anti-laminin-332 antibodies are present
Surveillance for scarring complications, including ocular fibrosis and airway and oesophageal stricture, by slit-lamp, nasendoscopy, laryngoscopy and endoscopy
Multidisciplinary care coordinating dermatology, ophthalmology, ENT, oral medicine and gastroenterology
Early escalation of immunosuppression for progressive scarring to prevent irreversible blindness or airway and oesophageal stenosis
